title: The Cost of Zero Cost
coreMove: Price the hidden costs of free before the zero overwhelms the better tradeoff.
sourcePressure: The source turns zero price into a special emotional category: people overvalue free offers because they feel safe from loss while other costs disappear.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says free is tempting; the chapter-specific lesson is that zero changes the perceived risk calculus and hides competing costs.

exampleSpecs.domain: airport lounge trial attached to a delayed flight
exampleSpecs.audience: a traveler deciding whether to accept a free lounge pass during a tight connection
exampleSpecs.stakes: missing the boarding-zone update because the free pass feels like found value
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the traveler writes the walk time to the far gate on the boarding pass before following the sign to the free lounge
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a boarding pass curled around a free lounge voucher at a crowded gate

exampleSpecs.domain: community garden offered free compost after a storm
exampleSpecs.audience: a plot holder choosing whether to haul extra compost she cannot use this month
exampleSpecs.stakes: losing a Saturday and blocking the shed path because zero price overrides storage reality
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she sets a tarp on the ground and marks the actual space her plot can absorb before loading another sack
exampleSpecs.firstImage: steaming compost sacks piled beside a bent garden gate

exampleSpecs.domain: local theater distributing free preview tickets
exampleSpecs.audience: a parent with one quiet evening deciding whether to accept four free seats
exampleSpecs.stakes: turning rest into logistics because tickets with no price feel too valuable to decline
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the parent writes the babysitter cost and drive time on the envelope before deciding whether the free tickets are still a gift
exampleSpecs.firstImage: four preview tickets tucked into a cream envelope on a hall table

exampleSpecs.domain: warehouse receiving free misprinted labels from a supplier
exampleSpecs.audience: an inventory supervisor deciding whether to accept a pallet of free labels
exampleSpecs.stakes: adding sorting errors because the labels cost nothing up front
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the supervisor traces three mis-shelved cartons back to the free label pallet and calculates the labor spent correcting them
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pallet of misprinted labels wrapped in cloudy plastic near dock door five

exampleSpecs.domain: pharmacy loyalty program offering a free vitamin bottle
exampleSpecs.audience: a caregiver picking up prescriptions before work
exampleSpecs.stakes: delaying needed pickup and buying unrelated items because the free bottle requires a second line
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the caregiver points to the prescription pickup clock and asks whether the free vitamin is worth the extra line before joining it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a bright loyalty coupon clipped to a prescription bag at the pharmacy counter

exampleSpecs.domain: public library giving away withdrawn atlases
exampleSpecs.audience: a youth-program coordinator tempted to take a box for map-craft workshops
exampleSpecs.stakes: using storage and planning time on materials that are free but stale
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before carrying the box, the teacher opens one atlas to the outdated map and names the exact lesson it would replace
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cardboard box of withdrawn atlases beside the library exit scanner

skillTargets: convert free into time, storage, attention, or risk costs
spot when zero price hides a worse alternative
distinguish a true gift from a costly obligation
evaluate whether loss aversion around paying is steering the choice

tryThisNowSpec: For one free offer in front of you, write the nonmoney cost in one concrete unit, such as minutes, shelf space, obligation, or delay, before accepting it.
